column3: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG)
column5: The Integrated Communities Strategy green paper invites views on the government’s vision for building strong integrated communities where people – whatever their background – live, work, learn and socialise together, based on shared rights, responsibilities and opportunities.
column6: The Green Paper includes recognition of the role that public libraries play in helping to bring diverse groups of people together in many different ways. Included is libraries’ current work on supporting and building communities, and their efforts in supporting social integration was fully acknowledged and celebrated. Work in Suffolk on Chat and Chill sessions, bringing people from different communities - explicitly migrant families - together was chosen to feature as a case study [page 46].[This consultation closes on 5 June 2018]

column5: Using technology to drive audience engagement, boosting the digital capability of cultural organisations and unleashing the creative potential of technology.

The Internet Safety Strategy looks at how government can ensure Britain is the safest place in the world to be online. The Strategy considers the responsibilities of companies to their users, the use of technical solutions to prevent online harms and government’s role in supporting users.
column6: The consultation included a section on libraries, including what the current offer is and what government will encourage them to do. This was to:- embed online safety aspects into existing library projects and events- run family learning sessions to help adults to support their children online- display online safety material and signpost resources for library staff, parents and children[DCMS is currently analysing feedback from the consultation]

column5: To support the development of the public library workforce in England, ensuring it continues to meet the changing needs of today’s audiences. This was in response to the action in Libraries Deliver: Ambition to produce a workforce development strategy.
column6: The strategy articulates a range of skills that staff and volunteers delivering public library services will need. It also outlines mechanisms for skills delivery and valuable support for employers. It will also help individuals develop their skills and plan careers; enabling them to succeed in a changing and competitive market.

column5: The strategy sets out how the government will build on its success to date to develop a world-leading digital economy that works for everyone.
column6: Libraries feature heavily in the digital skills and inclusion chapter. The has said it will government: - develop the role of libraries in improving digital inclusion to make them the ‘go-to’ provider of digital access training and support for local communities- We will bring together people from across sectors to collaborate and support the expansion of makerspaces in public libraries in EnglandThere is also a section on 'How libraries deliver improved digital access and literacy'

column1: Libraries Deliver: Ambition for Public Libraries in England 2016-2021
column5: Libraries Deliver: Ambition was published by the Libraries Taskforce in response to the Independent Library Report for England (December 2014) which called for a national strategy which articulated what public libraries in England are and why they are a force for good for us all. It sets out the government’s and Taskforce’s vision for, and commitment to, public libraries in England and provides a focus for joint action
column6: The document sets out a direction of travel for the next 5 years, describing how library services in England can help transform people, communities and society as a whole. Libraries Deliver: Ambition also provides a confirmation of how libraries support and add value to a range of local and national policy priorities and links to practical examples of existing good practice. It is supported by an action plan, saying what will happen to make the vision a reality

column5: This white paper sets out how the government will support cultural sectors over the coming years and how culture will play an active role in building a fairer and more prosperous nation that takes a lead on the international stage.
column6: The white paper describes how what we understand by culture has changed over time. "Culture no longer simply means being familiar with a select list of works of art and architecture, but the accumulated  influence of creativity, the arts, museums, galleries, libraries, archives and heritage upon all our lives. When we talk about our ‘cultural sectors’, we are referring to an extraordinary network of  individuals and organisations, that together preserve, reflect and promote who we are as a nation, in all our rich diversity."It particularly focuses on 4 areas of activity:- Everyone should enjoy the opportunities culture offers, no matter where they start in life- The riches of our culture should benefit communities across the country- The power of culture can increase our international standing- Cultural investment, resilience and reform

column5: Living Knowledge sets out the British Library’s vision for its future development.
column6: It sets out six core statements of purpose: custodianship, research, business, culture, learning and international and explains how the BL contributes to research, culture, education and economic prosperity, for the benefit not just of the UK but of users and partners around the world. Their mission is to make our intellectual heritage accessible to everyone, for research, inspiration and enjoyment.

column4: Independent panel led by William Sieghart
column5: The panel was jointly commissioned by DCMS and DCLG. Key questions for the panel to address included:- What are the core principles of a public library into the future?- Is the current model of delivery the most comprehensive and efficient? and- What is the role of community libraries?
column6: The panel emphasised the need for a re-invigoration of the library network. They identified a number of actions and made three major recommendations:1. The provision of a national digital resource for libraries, to be delivered in partnership with local authorities2. The setting up of a task and finish force, led by local government, in partnership with other bodies involved in the library sector, to provide a strategic framework for England, and to help in implementing the following3. The task force, to work with local authorities, to help them improve, revitalise and if necessary, change their local library service, while encouraging, appropriate to each library, increased community involvement

column1: The Modernisation Review of Public Libraries: A policy statement
column5: This policy paper followed the consultation initiated by DCMS in Empower, Inform, Enrich. The modernisation review of public libraries in November 2009. It addressed the five challenges raised in that document, and also added a sixth challenge: the variety in the quality of the library service across the country. This document built on Framework for the Future, by communicating and maximising the work of public libraries, and supporting the service to respond to those six challenges
column6: The proposals set out in the document covered a series of aims, with recommendations for action under each. The aims were:- to drive the quality of all library services up to the level ofthe best - to reverse the current trend of decline in library usage andgrow the numbers using the library service - that the library service is able to respond to limited publicresource and economic pressures - to ensure that all libraries respond to a 24/7 culture and tochanging expectations of people who want immediate access to information- that all libraries grasp the opportunities presented bydigitisation- to demonstrate to citizens, commentators and politiciansthat libraries are still relevant and vital

column1: Empower, Inform, Enrich. The modernisation review of public libraries: a consultation document
column5: The Review was established to question the structures, services and skills of the public library service to ensure that libraries are a major player in creating skilled, informed, creative citizens and communities for the 21st century.
column6: Five significant challenges were identiifed for the library service on which views were sought: • How can the library service demonstrate to citizens, commentators and politicians that they are still relevant and vital? • How can we reverse the current trend of decline in library usage and grow the numbers using their local library? • How can all libraries respond to a 24/7 culture and respond to changing expectations of people who want immediate access to information? • How can all libraries grasp the opportunities presented by digitisation? • How can the library service cope with limited public resource and economic pressures?There was a commitment to publish a policy statement in the spring which will set out the Government’s vision for the future of public libraries.

column1: Framework for the Future: Libraries, Learning and Information in the Next Decade
column4: DCMS with support from a project stakeholder group established in July 2002 ‘to guide the DCMS in the development of a new strategic framework for the public library service’.
column5: DCMS published Framework for the Future as a long-term strategic vision for the public library service. It was put together following extensive consultation with Resource (The Council for Museums, Archives andLibraries), the library community including the Advisory Council on Libraries, The CharteredInstitute of Library and Information Professionals, The Society of Chief Librarians and other keystakeholders in the education, community and voluntary sectors. The proposals were presented as a framework to encourage imaginative innovation and greater operational effectiveness and efficiency, adapted to local need and circumstance. Its purpose was to help local and library authorities agree on the key objectives for the public library service with central government and local communities.
column6: The document described how libraries needed a modern mission. They need constantly to renew and communicate their purpose to the communities they serve. Their modern mission should be based on:- Evolution: building on libraries’ traditional core skills in promoting reading, informal learning and self-help - Public value: focusing on areas where public intervention will deliver the largest benefits to society including support for adult literacy and pre-school learning- Distinctiveness: building on libraries’ open, neutral and self-help culture. They should not duplicate the efforts of other public and private sector providers but complement them through partnership working- Local interpretations of national programmes: developing national programmes which will raise the profile of the public library service as a whole but which are sufficiently flexible to be adapted to local needs. The document outlined the following three areas of activity which meet these criteria and should be at the heart of libraries’ modern mission:- The promotion of reading and informal learning- Access to digital skills and services including e-government- Measures to tackle social exclusion, build community identity and develop citizenship.

column2: July 1964 (Royal Assent); came fully into force 1 April 1965
column5: Provides the statutory framework for the delivery of public library services
column6: Local authorities have a statutory duty under the Public Libraries and Museums Act 1964 ‘to provide a comprehensive and efficient library service for all persons’ in the area that want to make use of it (section 7). Local authorities have the power to offer wider library services beyond the statutory service to other user groups, and the Act allows for joint working between library authorities.In providing this service, local authorities must, among other things:- have regard to encouraging both adults and children to make full use of the library service (section 7(2)(b))- lend books and other printed material free of charge for those who live, work or study in the area (section 8(3)(b))It is the statutory duty of the Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport to:- superintend, and promote the improvement of, the public library service provided by local authorities in England (section 1(1))- secure the proper discharge by local authorities of the functions in relation to libraries conferred on them as library authoritiesThe Secretary of State has the power to make a remedial order against a library authority following a local inquiry. Such an inquiry can be commenced either on receipt of a complaint that a local library authority is failing to carry out its statutory duties or of the Secretary of State’s own motion (section 10).

column3: Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe
column4: Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe
column5: To show how libraries and museums act as a resource for human development and lifelong learning with the growing importance of the knowledge economy in Europe.
column6: Looked at: the new and expanding role and the economic pressures and challenges of musuems and libraries and the future of making them resilient and sustainable. The Assembly made a series of recommendations to the EU member States which emphasised the importance to recognise the social, economic and cultural value of libraries and museums, to support and fund their work financially and strategically by providing "sufficient autonomy to directly manage their staff and budget" and supporting their position as centres for digital education - including providing free internet access.
